narrative: The model estimated a 64.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means, on the evidence reviewed, failure was judged more likely than passing; your admission was denied because the school uses that bar-risk prediction in its decision, not because passing is impossible. The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in decile 1, while accepted students averaged about decile 5.8, and this was the largest push toward a fail prediction. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor; at 20, compared with an accepted-student average of 37.18, it also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, and its influence actually worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing, even though your 2.70 is below the accepted average of 3.23. Thus the denial was driven mainly by very low third-year rank and LSAT, partly offset by GPA. Next, seek specific admissions feedback; address the LSAT with structured preparation and a retake; consider additional coursework or a graduate credential to demonstrate academic readiness; and reapply only after you can show stronger evidence, especially in LSAT performance and upper-level academic rank.
